config.title: Trapping Rain Water

intro.title: Trapping Rain Water
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function to calculate how much rainwater can be trapped between bars of different heights, a classic lesson in algorithm design. You will learn the core concept of using two pointers to efficiently scan the array from both ends, comparing heights to determine water capacity at each position. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, loops, conditional logic, and the two-pointer technique. By the end, you will understand how to solve this lesson step-by-step and implement a working solution in JavaScript.
intro.usecase: The Trapping Rain Water algorithm is essential in real-world applications like urban planning software, where it helps model water accumulation in terrain or city landscapes to design effective drainage systems. In data visualization dashboards, this pattern can be used to represent resource allocation or capacity limits, such as showing storage usage peaks in cloud infrastructure monitoring tools. Developers implement similar logic in UI components like progress bars or gauges that need to calculate filled areas between boundaries, ensuring accurate visual representations of constrained metrics.

objectives: Implement the two-pointer approach to calculate trapped rainwater
Construct a function that iterates through elevation data using left and right pointers
Manipulate pointer positions based on elevation comparisons
Initialize variables to track maximum heights on both sides
Apply conditional logic to determine water accumulation at each position
Integrate the algorithm to process elevation arrays of varying lengths
Render the total trapped water value after processing the input

content.body: Imagine rainwater trapped between buildings of different heights. How much water can be stored? This classic lesson, Trapping Rain Water, teaches us to think in terms of boundaries and remember what we've seen. We'll solve it efficiently using array scanning and lookup structures.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply the two-pointer technique to track left and right boundaries.
• Implement a single-pass solution using a lookup structure to store maximum heights.
• Explain why storing and checking boundary heights prevents redundant calculations.

content.body: You just performed a manual scan: for each position, you looked left and right to find the highest boundaries, then calculated water as the minimum boundary minus current height. This requires checking all positions repeatedly.
content.title: What you did

content.body: For an array of 10,000 buildings, scanning left and right for every position becomes extremely slow (O(n²)). We need a method that remembers boundary heights as we go, avoiding re-scanning. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of rescanning, we can store the maximum height seen so far from the left and right in separate arrays or variables. This is like keeping a notebook of the tallest building we've encountered from each direction.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down the tallest building seen from the left and right as we walk along the skyline.

content.body: We'll use two passes to precompute left and right maximums, then a single pass to calculate water. Alternatively, we can use two pointers and track maxima dynamically.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For heights [3,0,2,0,4]:
1. Left max array: [3,3,3,3,4] (tallest so far from left).
2. Right max array: [4,4,4,4,4] (tallest so far from right).
3. For each i: water += min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) - height[i].
Result: 3+0+1+0+0 = 4? Wait, let's recalculate carefully.
Actually, water at index 1: min(3,4)-0=3; index 2: min(3,4)-2=1; index 3: min(3,4)-0=3; total = 7.

content.body:
1. Initialize left and right pointers at both ends.
2. Track leftMax and rightMax (starting at 0).
3. Move the pointer pointing to the shorter building.
4. For current position: if height < currentMax, add water (currentMax - height); else update currentMax.
5. Repeat until pointers meet.

steps.title: Set up function and variables
steps.instruction: Create the function trap that takes height array. Initialize left and right pointers, leftMax and rightMax to 0, and totalWater to 0.
steps.hint: Use let for variables that will change.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the pointers and tracking variables.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure to declare all four variables: left, right, leftMax, rightMax, and totalWater.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start fresh. Declare left=0, right=height.length-1, leftMax=0, rightMax=0, totalWater=0.

steps.title: Create the main loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues while left pointer is less than right pointer.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The loop will run until pointers meet.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the condition: it should be left < right.

steps.title: Compare heights and move pointer
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, compare height[left] and height[right]. If left side is shorter, process left pointer; else process right pointer.
steps.expectedOutcome: Conditional added to decide which pointer to process.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good! This decides which boundary to expand.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure to compare height[left] and height[right].

steps.title: Process left pointer
steps.instruction: In the if block, check if height[left] >= leftMax. If yes, update leftMax; else add water (leftMax - height[left]) to totalWater.
steps.hint: Remember: water is added only when current height is less than the max from that side.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're correctly updating max or adding water.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check both cases: update leftMax if height[left] >= leftMax, else add to totalWater.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: if (height[left] >= leftMax) leftMax = height[left]; else totalWater += leftMax - height[left]; left++;

steps.title: Process right pointer and return
steps.instruction: In the else block, do the symmetric for right side: update rightMax or add water,
steps.hint: Mirror the left side logic but use rightMax and decrement right.
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete function with right side handling and return.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the two-pointer solution.

content.body: You've successfully implemented the Trapping Rain Water solution! Remember: the key is to track the maximum heights from both sides as you go, using two pointers to avoid extra passes. This 'remember what we've seen' pattern—storing boundaries in variables—is powerful for many array lessons. Keep practicing this mental model!
